We can issue tokens representing ownership of the building, on the blockchain.” I found this very confusing. In fact, for decades, it has been possible to issue shares of a commercial building. It’s traditionally called a “REIT,” a real estate investment trust; most REITs have lots of buildings, but a single-building REIT is possible . There are plenty of REITs listed on US stock exchanges. What did crypto bring to the table? I thought there were three main answers: Technology: Maybe tokens on a blockchain are faster, more efficient, more modern, more 24/7, etc., than shares listed on the stock exchange. Legality: Shares of a REIT — shares of anything, really — are securities under US law, and selling them to the general public requires registration with the US Securities and Exchange Commission, financial statements, disclosure, etc. Many people think this is a good thing — it’s good for investors to know the legally required information about the building they are buying shares in — but crypto people generally thought it was a bad thing, and preferred to avoid SEC registration. Perhaps issuing “tokens” rather than “shares” would avoid the registration requirements. Gambling: It always struck me that, while there was a lot of enthusiasm from crypto founders to tokenize real estate, there was never any obvious enthusiasm from anyone for buying shares of buildings. The thing is, every two years, prediction markets are amazing . Every normal American wants to know one thing when the polls close on Election Day, which is “who won?” You can go on social media, and people who are abnormally addicted to politics will be posting stuff like “watch the results in XY-23, that was R +13.5 in ’24, if it’s within two points then the Rs are going to have a long night,” and you can be like “ah, yes, I will be sure to watch those results,” and then someone else will post “the latest early ballot drop in PQ-7 has way more shy NC WWCs than expected, it’s going to be a long night for the Ds,” and you’re like “ah I see,” and various news sites will be calling races with 0.3% of the votes counted, and there will be a vast mosaic of information that you can, with great effort and attention, piece together to get a picture of how the evening is going. And if that’s fun for you, great. Clearly a lot of people consume this stuff as entertainment. But I personally am busy and nervous and like to go to bed early, and it would be nice if someone else would piece everything together, weight it appropriately by how much it matters, and generate one simple answer to the question “who won?” [1] Obviously, 20 minutes after the polls close, that answer will not be definitive. But instead of me frantically looking at all the data points as they come in and updating my expectations about who won, someone else should do that and just tell me the most likely answer and the degree of confidence. We have talked a few times about pre-IPO perpetual futures: Some offshore trading platforms, most notably Hyperliquid/Trade[XYZ], [1] list perpetual futures contracts on big private companies that are approaching their initial public offerings. These contracts are bets on the future price of the stock, and it is not at all obvious that the futures price would closely track the actual stock value: The perps do not represent any claim on the underlying stock, they are in theory off-limits to investors in the US, existing shareholders of the underlying companies are probably not allowed to sell the perps to hedge their exposure, big institutional investors who might want to buy shares in the IPO are probably not set up to buy the perps to anticipate their demand, etc. The perps are in a sense just a recreational prediction market on the price of the stock, not a derivative instrument tied to the price of the stock by arbitrage mechanisms. But a really important thing we have learned about finance in the last few years is that prediction markets are pretty accurate. Is there anything you can do about it? At a high level, there are two somewhat reassuring answers: Your bank might be able to get the money back. “Stealing your money,” in this context, means basically moving some money from your bank’s electronic ledger representing your account to another bank’s electronic ledger representing the thief’s account. Your bank can call the thief’s bank and be like “that was theft, give us our money back,” and the thief’s bank probably will. Banks are quasi-law-enforcement agencies, and they will cooperate to reverse fraud or theft. On the other hand, the theft might be irreversible. The thief might have moved the money to another bank, and then withdrawn it in cash from the other bank, used the cash to buy art or casino chips, and rendered the money untraceable and removed from the electronic system allowing its recovery. In that case, you’re not necessarily out of luck. Your bank might be out of luck. Your bank is required to have good cybersecurity controls, prevent theft, etc., and if it messes this up it will probably have to reimburse you . This means, effectively, that the bank’s shareholders have to reimburse you. The bank has, like, $100 billion of money in its electronic ledgers, of which like $90 billion belongs to depositors like you and $10 billion belongs to its shareholders. (The $10 billion is the bank’s “capital,” and the law requires banks to have at least some minimum level of capital as a percentage of assets.) If the bank loses $100 of your money, it might have to subtract $100 from its shareholders’ money and add that back to yours. You are protected. These answers are in various ways imperfect. There are scenarios where the bank might not have to reimburse you. (The term of art is that banks need to reimburse you for “fraud,” but not for “scams.” ) And you could imagine really bad forms of hacking — where the hackers take all of the bank’s money, or where the bank loses its ledger of accounts entirely — where these solutions wouldn’t work. The fund owned some Lehman Brothers securities, and when Lehman filed for bankruptcy those securities lost value and Reserve concluded that its assets were worth only $0.97 per share. It had “broken the buck”; investors who had expected the fund to always be worth $1 per share were now disappointed. Investors demanded their money back, and Reserve had to close down, liquidate the fund, and give all of its investors back their money at a loss. Ultimately it paid them $0.991 per share. They lost 0.9% of their money. This was a huge scandal . It doesn’t seem that huge? But this was all quite rational. You see, if Reserve had cashed out all of its investors at $1 when they asked for their money back, the first investors to get cashed out would all get back $1 and have no losses, but eventually the money would run out, and the last investors left in the fund would get back $0 and have 100% losses. That’s what a bank run is. The last 0.9% of investors would have had 100% losses. The other 99.1% of investors would have been perfectly fine. In some abstract sense, if you were an investor in the fund, you had a 99.1% chance of being fine, so there was really no need to rush to get your money out.
